title: Phosphorus‐Modified Siderite/nZVI Composite for Peroxymonosulfate Activation and Sulfamethoxazole Degradation in Groundwater
content:
Phosphorus modification regulates the siderite/nZVI interface to enhance PMS adsorption and activation, enabling rapid sulfamethoxazole degradation in real groundwater. SMX oxidation proceeds through coupled radical and nonradical pathways, with SO₄•− as the dominant radical species and 1O2 also contributing.


ABSTRACT

Sulfamethoxazole (SMX) contamination in groundwater has attracted increasing concern because of its potential ecological risks. In this study, a phosphorus-modified siderite/nanoscale zero-valent iron composite (P@FFC) was developed for peroxymonosulfate (PMS) activation and SMX degradation in real groundwater. Under the standard conditions of an initial SMX concentration of 5 mg L−1, a PMS concentration of 4 mM, a P@FFC dosage of 0.6 g L−1, an initial pH of 5.0, and a temperature of 25°C, 98.34% SMX removal was achieved within 4 min. The apparent rate constant increased from 0.0122 min−1 for FFC/PMS to 0.887 min−1 for P@FFC/PMS. A TOC removal of 60.49% was achieved within 35 min, indicating substantial mineralization. Characterization and DFT calculations suggested that phosphorus modification regulated the catalyst interface by increasing surface roughness, introducing P–O-containing surface species, and promoting PMS adsorption. ROS analyses revealed coupled radical and nonradical pathways. SO4 •− was the major radical species, while •OH and 1O2 were also involved and O2 •− played a limited role. Rapid SMX degradation was also retained in unadjusted groundwater. Although catalytic activity declined during repeated use, Fe and P leaching remained limited. NaBH4 treatment partially restored the activity of used P@FFC. These results provide insight into phosphorus-mediated interfacial regulation during PMS activation and support the potential of P@FFC for groundwater remediation.
